project.name: Crumbs
project.tagline: A small language. Straight to C.
project.description: Crumbs is a small, statically typed, C-style toy programming language implemented in Python. It compiles Crumbs source into a single C translation unit, then builds that output with GCC or Clang.

quickstart.description: Compile and run a source file.
Run the type checker without building.

sections.description: Install python>=3.14, git and curl before running this command!

features.title: Dependencies
features.desc: Crumbs rely on dependencies to run, due to it being written in python. You first need to install the needed dependencies before running crumbs
features.command: sudo apt install python3 clang git curl

features.desc: Clone the repo and get the source code of crumbs

features.title: Creation
features.desc: Create a project in a new directory (`--lib` for a library), or turn the current directory into one with `init`.

features.title: Build
features.desc: Compile the project. `--release` picks the release profile; every option is forwarded to the compiler under its real name.

features.title: Run
features.desc: Compile and run. Arguments after `--` go to your program.

features.title: Check, emit, clean
features.desc: Type-check only, print the generated C, or delete the build directory.

features.title: See what it does
features.desc: `-n` prints the exact compiler command, `-v` logs time spent lexing, parsing, checking and generating code, `-vv` adds a per-file table. `cookie info` shows the commands for each profile.

features.title: Profiles and defaults
features.desc: Settings merge as command line > profile > [build] > default. Debug builds with -O0 and overflow panics; release builds with -O3. Unknown keys are reported with a suggestion.

sections.title: Basics
sections.description: The core syntax used in everyday Crumbs programs.

features.title: Importing Modules
features.desc: Use `import` to load another Crumbs module. A dotted module path maps to a file path: `import std.math;` loads the standard math module. The module name is its final path segment unless an alias is provided.
features.code:
import std.math;
import std.conv as conv;
features.note: Only `pub` items are visible to importing modules. Import cycles are rejected.

features.title: Defining Functions
features.desc: Declare functions with `fn`, typed parameters, and an optional return type. The return type follows `->`. Every non-void function must return on every path.

features.title: Named and default arguments
features.desc: Give a parameter a default with `= literal` (a number, string, `true`/`false` or `null`). Parameters with defaults come last, and a caller may leave them out. After the positional arguments, any argument can be passed by name, in any order, which is handy to skip a default in the middle. This works for every function and method declared with `fn`; function pointers and C variadics take positional arguments only. A missing argument, an unknown or duplicated name and a non-literal default are compile errors.

features.title: Variables and Mutability
features.desc: Variables are immutable by default. Add `mut` when a binding needs to be reassigned or changed. Local types can often be inferred from the initializer.

features.title: Declaring Constants
features.desc: Declare a named constant with `const`. Constants have an explicit type and an initializer.

features.title: For Loops
features.desc: A `for` loop iterates over a range, array, slice, or string. `0..N` excludes the upper bound; `0..=N` includes it.

features.title: Loop Control
features.desc: Use `break` to leave a loop and `continue` to skip to its next iteration. Destructors are also run when control leaves a scope through `break` or `continue`.

features.title: Conditional Branches
features.desc: Conditions must be `bool`. Use `if` and `else` blocks to select which statements execute.

features.title: Pattern Matching
features.desc: `match` selects a branch based on a value. Matches over enums must be exhaustive, so every variant needs to be handled.

sections.title: Types
sections.description: Built-in types, methods, generics, traits, and numeric conversions.

features.title: Primitive Types
features.desc: Crumbs provides signed and unsigned integers (`i8` through `i64`, `u8` through `u64`), `f32`, `f64`, `bool`, `str`, `String`, and `void`.

features.title: Arrays and Slices
features.desc: `[N]T` is a fixed-size array and `[]T` is a slice. Indexing accesses an element; slicing creates a view. Slice bounds and ranges are checked at runtime.

features.title: Structs and Enums
features.desc: Define records with `struct` and a finite set of variants with `enum`. Struct fields and function parameters carry explicit types.

features.title: Pointers and Dereferencing
features.desc: A `*T` is a pointer to `T` and may be null. Take an address with `&`, dereference with `*`, and use `as` for explicit pointer or integer casts. Dereferencing null panics with a source location. Fields and methods are reached straight through a pointer: `level.player.x`, `level.get_block(x, y)`. `p->x` and `p->f()` are the C spelling of `(*p).x` and `(*p).f()`.

features.title: impl blocks
features.desc: Declare functions on a type: `Point.new(1, 2)`, `p.sum()`. `self` borrows the value, `mut self` mutates it (the variable must be `let mut`), and `Self` names the type inside the block. A field holding a function pointer wins over a method of the same name. `String`, `str` and `List<T>` have their methods with no import.

features.title: Generic and built-in impls
features.desc: A generic struct's `impl` repeats its type parameters. Methods can also be added to built-in types such as `String` and `str`.

features.title: Generic Functions
features.desc: Generic functions are monomorphized: each distinct type instantiation produces specialized C code. Type arguments are inferred from call arguments or can be written explicitly.
features.note: Bodies are checked once per instantiation, so without a bound any operation the body uses must work for the chosen types. Add a trait bound (see Traits) to state what a type parameter must be able to do, and have the compiler check it at the call.

features.title: Generic Structs
features.desc: Structs can declare type parameters. Crumbs can infer generic struct arguments from initialized fields or an expected type.

features.title: Declaring and implementing a trait
features.desc: A trait lists the methods a type must have. `impl Trait for Type` supplies them. The compiler checks that every required method is present, that nothing extra is added, and that each signature (receiver, parameter types, return type) matches the declaration. Structs, enums and built-in types can all implement traits, and the trait and the implementing type may live in different modules.
features.note: A trait is not a type: write `fn f<T: Shape>(x: T)`, not `fn f(x: Shape)`. Dispatch is static (monomorphized), so there is no runtime cost and no trait objects.

features.title: Trait bounds
features.desc: Put bounds on type parameters with `T: Trait`, or `T: A + B` for several. Bounds work on generic functions, generic structs and generic `impl` blocks, and are checked at every instantiation, whether the type arguments are inferred or written out. A failed bound reports which type, which trait and where the bound was declared. An impl can itself be conditional: `impl<T: Shape> Shape for Labelled<T>` applies only when `T` is a `Shape`.
features.note: error: the trait bound `Dot: Shape` is not satisfied -- required by the bound `T: Shape` on the function `total`.

features.title: Default methods and supertraits
features.desc: A trait method with a body is a default: an `impl` may leave it out and gets the default, or override it. Inside a default, `Self` is the implementing type, so it can call the trait's other methods. `trait Solid: Shape` makes `Shape` a supertrait: every `Solid` type must also implement `Shape`, and the compiler says so when it does not. Supertrait cycles are rejected.

features.title: Showing your own types: Display
features.desc: `println`, `to_str` and `"{x}"` know how to show numbers, text, bools and enum names. To show a struct, or to change how an enum looks, implement the prelude trait `Display` (no import needed): its one method `to_string(self) -> String` is what `println(x)` prints and what `{x}` inserts, and the format spec (width, fill, alignment) then applies to that text. Types without an impl can still be shown with `{x:?}`, the automatic representation: `Point { x: 3, y: -4 }`, with arrays as `[1, 2]` and text quoted. `T: Display` works as a bound, and the numeric types and `bool` implement it. Showing a struct without either is a compile error that says which to add. `Duration` and `DateTime` from `std.time` are Display.

features.title: Implicit Numeric Conversions
features.desc: Lossless widening conversions happen silently. Mixed numeric operators use a common type that can represent both operands. Narrowing or sign-changing assignments are allowed with a runtime range check and a warning.

features.title: Explicit Type Casts
features.desc: Use `as` for explicit conversions, including truncating casts. Conversions such as float-to-integer and number-to-pointer require an explicit cast. `--strict-casts` promotes conversion warnings to errors.

features.title: Wrapping Arithmetic
features.desc: Normal integer arithmetic is overflow-checked. The wrapping operators `+%`, `-%`, and `*%` wrap instead of panicking, and wrapping compound assignments are available too.

features.title: Integer overflow
features.desc: `+ - *` and unary `-` wrap around in two's complement by default. `--overflow-panic` turns overflow into a panic with a source location (the cookie debug profile does this). Division by zero always panics; `MIN / -1` wraps unless `--overflow-panic` is on.

sections.title: Errors and memory
sections.description: Typed error handling, ownership-like moves, strings, allocation, and optional garbage collection.

features.title: Error Types and Values
features.desc: `T!` represents either a value of type `T` or an error. Define named error values with `error`, and raise one with `throw`.

features.title: Error Propagation and Handling
features.desc: Use `try` to propagate an error to the caller. Use `catch` to supply a fallback value or handle the error with a handler that must diverge.

features.title: String Views and Owned Strings
features.desc: `str` is an immutable byte-string view. `String` is an owned, growable heap string with a destructor. Strings support appending, concatenation, indexing, slicing, and conversion to `str` where a borrow is valid.

features.title: Format strings
features.desc: `println`, `print`, `format`, `panic` and the message of `assert` take a template as their first argument, written the way Rust does it. `{}` takes the next argument, `{0}` a numbered one, `{name}` a named argument (`name = value`) or else the variable of that name (`{p.x}` reaches fields); `{{` and `}}` are literal braces. `{x:spec}` formats the value. `format(...)` returns an owned `String`; the others print or panic with the text. Expressions go in the argument list, not inside the braces. The spec is `[[fill]align][sign][#][0][width][,|_][.precision][type]`: align is `<` `>` `^`; sign is `+` or a space; `#` adds `0x` `0b` `0o`; `0` pads numbers with zeros; `,` or `_` group digits; precision is digits after the point for floats and a maximum length for text; the type is `d x X b o c` for integers, `f F e E g G` for floats and `?` for the automatic representation. Mistakes in a template or spec, unused arguments and missing arguments are compile errors.
features.note: A template without braces still prints extra values one after another (`println("n = ", n)`). Text is counted in characters, so `{:>7}` pads "héllo" correctly. Negative numbers in `x`, `b` and `o` show a minus sign and the magnitude. Format strings need the standard runtime (not `--no-stdruntime`).

features.title: Destructors and Move Semantics
features.desc: Define a destructor with `drop TypeName(self)`. Values with destructors are moved rather than copied, and the compiler tracks moved values to prevent later use. Destructors run when values leave scope, including on return and error propagation.

features.title: Heap Allocation
features.desc: `alloc(T, n)` allocates a slice of `n` elements and `free` releases it. Allocation failure is checked by the runtime. `free` can also release an owned `String` early.

features.title: Generational garbage collector
features.desc: The default collector has three generations. New blocks are born in the nursery (generation 0). A minor collection looks only at the nursery and moves survivors to generation 1; a mid collection covers generations 0 and 1 and moves survivors to generation 2 (old); a major collection traces everything and sweeps the old generation lazily as you allocate. Most blocks die young, so most collections touch only a small part of the heap. It is conservative (stacks, registers and the data segment are scanned for anything that looks like a pointer), thread-aware, and managed blocks include `alloc()` memory, `String` buffers and the string arena. Explicit `free` and destructors stay valid. `--no-gc` switches to plain malloc. When collections run is your choice: see the collector modes below.
features.note: Pointers kept only on the C side are not visible to the collector: keep a Crumbs reference to memory that C must retain. C code that stores Crumbs pointers into Crumbs memory should call `cb_gc_write_barrier(p, size)` afterwards.

features.title: Collector modes: auto, thread and manual
features.desc: `--gc-mode` chooses who decides when to collect. `auto` (the default) collects from inside the allocator when the nursery fills, so nothing needs configuring. `thread` is for beginners who want it hands-off: a background collector thread wakes every `--gc-interval` milliseconds (default 100) and collects whatever has accumulated, so allocating code never pauses to collect and you never call anything. The compiler adds a cheap safepoint check to every function entry and loop iteration so the collector can stop your threads promptly; sleeping and waiting for input are safepoints too. `manual` is for advanced users: the collector never runs by itself, and you decide when with `gc_collect()` and `gc_collect_gen(g)`. `gc_collect_gen` exists only in manual mode, so ordinary programs never need to know about generations. Set it in `project.toml` with `gc_mode` and `gc_interval`.
features.command:
crumbs run app.cb --gc-mode=thread --gc-interval=50
crumbs run app.cb --gc-mode=manual
features.note: In `auto` and `thread` mode `gc_collect_gen` is a compile error that points to `--gc-mode=manual`. In manual mode memory grows until you collect. Thread mode adds a polling check to loops; use `auto` for the tightest numeric kernels.

features.title: How generations stay correct
features.desc: A minor collection must still find old blocks that point at young ones. The compiler emits a write barrier after every store of a pointer-holding value through a pointer, slice, field or `write_at`; it marks a 512-byte card dirty, and the next minor or mid collection scans the dirty cards as extra roots. Programs that never store into old memory pay almost nothing. Build with `--cflag=-DCB_GC_VERIFY` to check every collection against a full trace of the heap: a missed barrier aborts with a message. Tuning macros: `CB_GC_NURSERY`, `CB_GC_MID`, `CB_GC_MID_EVERY`, `CB_GC_MAJOR_MIN`, `CB_GC_CARD_BUDGET`.

features.title: Collector controls and statistics
features.desc: `gc_collect()` forces a major collection in every mode. `gc_collect_gen(g)` collects generations `0..g` (0 minor, 1 mid, 2 major) and is available only with `--gc-mode=manual`. `gc_bytes()` reports live bytes, `gc_collections()` counts all cycles, and `gc_gen_bytes(g)` / `gc_gen_collections(g)` report one generation in every mode. All are no-ops returning 0 with `--no-gc`.

features.title: Regions (scoped lifetimes)
features.desc: `region r { ... alloc_in(T, n, r) ... }` frees everything in one step on every way out of the block. Region memory is never traced or swept object by object, so it does not wake the collector, but live regions are scanned as roots. The compiler rejects returning or storing region memory where it would outlive the region.

features.title: Freestanding builds
features.desc: `--no-stdruntime` emits only integer and bounds helpers: no libc, no `print`, `String`, `alloc`, collector, regions or `std.*` (except `std.mem`). Use it with `--entry=` and `export fn` to produce an object file with no libc symbols.

sections.title: Standard library
sections.description: The standard library is written in Crumbs and imported with `std.*` module paths. Related modules are grouped on one page each.

features.title: What is in std
features.desc: `std.io` input and output; `std.list` and `std.mem` collections and helpers; `std.str`, `std.conv`, `std.math` and `std.rand` text, numbers and randomness; `std.time` clocks and dates; `std.fs` and `std.env` files and the environment; `std.thread` threads and channels. `std.fmt` holds the `Display` trait. `String`, `str`, `List<T>` and `Display` need no import. `std.time`, `std.fs`, `std.env`, `std.io` and `std.thread` contain no C helpers: they bind libc and pthread with ordinary `extern fn` declarations, exactly like user code.

features.title: Standard Input and Output
features.desc: The I/O module provides character input and output, line input, and flushing. Input operations that can fail return an error union.

features.title: Growable Lists
features.desc: `list.List<T>` is a growable array that owns its elements. It supports primitive values, strings, structs, arrays, function pointers, and nested lists. Elements are released automatically when the list is released or leaves scope.

features.title: List API
features.desc: `new`, `with_capacity`, `from_slice`, `push`, `pop` (`T!`, error `Empty`), `at` (a pointer, any `T`), `get`, `set`, `insert`, `remove`, `swap_remove`, `extend`, `view`, `clear`, `release`, `reverse`, `sort_by(l, cmp)` (heap sort, `cmp` like C's `qsort`), `for_each`, `find_by`.

features.title: std.mem
features.desc: Generic helpers: `swap`, `min`, `max`, `sort`. Usable in freestanding builds.

features.title: std.str
features.desc: Trimming, `find`/`rfind`, `split`, `join`, `replace`, case conversion and comparison. Every `str` function also works on a `String`.
features.code:
import std.str;

println(str.trim("  hi  "), str.upper("abc"));

features.title: std.conv, std.math, std.rand
features.desc: `std.conv` converts between text and numbers, `std.math` has the usual numeric functions (`gcd`, `tan`, ...), and `std.rand` generates random numbers.

features.title: Clocks, durations and calendar dates
features.desc: `monotonic_ns()`, `unix()`, `unix_ms()`, `sleep_ms(n)`; `Duration` (`from_ms`, `as_secs_f64`, `to_string()`), `Stopwatch` (`start`, `elapsed`, `lap`, `reset`), and calendar dates: `from_unix`, `now_utc`, `now_local`, `DateTime.new(y, m, d, h, mi, s)`, `.format()`, `.iso()`, `.weekday_name()`, `.add_days(n)`, `is_leap_year`, `days_in_month`.

features.title: std.fs
features.desc: `read_to_string`, `read_lines`, `write`, `append`, `exists`, `is_file`, `is_dir`, `size`, `remove`, `make_dir`. Errors: `NotFound`, `IoError`.
features.code:
import std.fs;

let text = fs.read_to_string("notes.txt") catch |e| { panic("missing"); };

features.title: std.env
features.desc: `args()`, `arg(i)`, `arg_count()`, `get(name)` (error `NotSet`) and `has(name)`.

features.title: std.thread
features.desc: `spawn(f, arg)` / `spawn_fn(f)` return a `Thread` (`.join()`); `Mutex` (`lock`, `try_lock`, `unlock`); `Condvar` (`wait`, `signal`, `broadcast`); `AtomicI64`; the generic `channel<T>()` (`send`, `recv`, `close`; error `Closed`); `sleep_ms`, `yield_now`, `current_id`, `cpu_count`. The collector waits for other threads to reach an allocation or a blocking call before it runs.

sections.title: C interoperability
sections.description: Call C libraries and expose Crumbs functions through declarations in the source file.

features.title: External Functions and Structs
features.desc: Declare C functions and data with `extern`. An external struct uses C layout; opaque external structs can be used behind pointers. Symbol names can be aliased.

features.title: Linking and Exporting Symbols
features.desc: Use `link` to add a library or object/source file. Use `export fn` to give a Crumbs function a plain C name so external C code can call it. Command-line alternatives include `-l`, `-L`, `--link`, and `--pkg`.

features.title: C Interoperability Helpers
features.desc: Bridge helpers include `cstr`, `from_cstr`, `.ptr`, `slice_of`, and `size_of`. Only types with a C equivalent can cross the boundary.

sections.title: Compiler and safety
sections.description: The compiler pipeline, diagnostics, runtime checks, and current language limits.

features.title: Compiler Commands
features.desc: The command-line driver can run, build, emit generated C, or type-check a source file. GCC and Clang are supported as C compilers.
features.command:
crumbs run examples/hello.cb
crumbs build examples/hello.cb -o hello
crumbs emit examples/hello.cb
crumbs check examples/hello.cb

features.title: Build Options
features.desc: Useful options include `--unchecked` to remove overflow and bounds checks, `-O3` for optimization, `--cc clang` to select the C compiler, `--keep-c` to retain generated C, `--entry` to choose an entry function, `--no-gc` to turn the collector off, and `--cflag` to pass a flag to the C compiler.
features.command:
crumbs build main.cb \
    --unchecked -O3 --cc clang --keep-c out.c

crumbs build library.cb --entry=

features.title: Compile-Time Safety Checks
features.desc: The checker enforces initialization, mutability, boolean conditions, complete returns, exhaustive matches, and handling of error unions. It also diagnoses invalid constant bounds, division by a literal zero, and unused or unreachable code.

features.title: Runtime Safety Checks
features.desc: The runtime panics with a source location and exit code 101 for integer overflow, division by zero, array/slice/string bounds, invalid slice ranges, invalid shift amounts, and allocation failure.
features.code:
let values = [1, 2, 3];
println(values[8]); // bounds panic
